title: Dialogue: The heartbeat of instructional coaching
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes argues that instructional coaching's greatest risk is becoming a one-sided monologue - a coach 'talking at' the coachee - which she identifies as a lethal mutation of models like Bambrick-Santoyo's 'Praise, Probe'. She grounds the case for genuine dialogue in cognitive science, arguing coaching conversation surfaces mental models (Johnson-Laird), supports schema construction (Sweller), promotes metacognition (Flavell), strengthens retrieval and transfer (Agarwal and Bain), and enables error detection through feedback loops (Hattie and Timperley). She cites the 2018 Kraft, Blazar and Hogan meta-analysis of 60 studies showing coaching's effect size rivals the difference between a novice and a five-to-ten-year veteran teacher, and closes with concrete techniques - using video scenarios and 'approximations' (low-stakes rehearsals) - to bring genuine dialogic coaching to life.
points: Hughes's central warning - that coaching frameworks like Praise-Probe can mutate into a monologue where 'the coachee can only nod' - names a common but underdiagnosed failure mode in instructional coaching implementation.

She grounds dialogue's value in five distinct cognitive science mechanisms (mental model surfacing, schema construction, metacognition, retrieval/transfer, error detection via feedback), not just a general appeal to 'good conversation'.

Her citation of the 2018 Kraft, Blazar and Hogan meta-analysis (coaching's effect size rivalling five to ten years of added teaching experience) grounds the case for coaching investment in strong evidence.
Her concrete techniques - video-based decision scenarios and low-stakes 'approximation' rehearsals
translate the theoretical argument into practices coaches can use immediately.
quotes: A 2018 meta-analysis of 60 studies showed that instructional coaching has large positive effects on both instructional practice and student achievement: The quality of teachers' instruction improves by as much as - or more than - the difference in effectiveness between a novice and a teacher with five to 10 years of experience.

One of the biggest lethal mutations I see of this model is that it becomes a checklist to be worked through as quickly as possible, which inevitably means that coaches/mentors just talk at their coachee/mentee for 15 minutes.
Mental models are internal representations that guide how individuals interpret and respond to situations. Through dialogue, coaches help teachers make their implicit reasoning explicit.

Lofthouse and Hall introduced the idea of the coaching dialogic space - a professional environment characterised by trust, openness and curiosity. Within this space, teachers can test ideas, process emotions and take professional risks.
So the next time we think about improving teaching, let's start with a conversation, because when we talk, we think. When we think better, we teach better.
